title: Opportunity Cost: Studying, Transit, and Work
topic: Explain opportunity cost using a college student choosing among studying, commuting, and part-time work.

segments.text: Opportunity cost measures the value of the best alternative you give up whenever scarce time or money forces a choice.
In college, my scarcest resource is weekday evenings. Between commuting, a part-time shift, and studying, something always gets cut.
Trace one typical evening block. Once transit eats an hour, the remaining window forces a direct trade-off between wages and exam prep.

segments.text: Hold on—what if a student genuinely needs the shift wages to pay for next week's fare? Isn't calling that a cost misleading?
That is a sharp distinction. Taking the shift can still be the rational decision; opportunity cost does not mean the choice was wrong.
So economists separate explicit costs like bus fare from implicit costs like the study hours you gave up?
Correct. When you evaluate a decision carefully, follow three quick steps so you only count the single next-best option.

steps.label: List feasible choices
steps.description: Identify what actually fits your open hours

steps.label: Rank the next-best
steps.description: Pick the single strongest alternative you skip

steps.label: Compare full payoff
steps.description: Weigh both cash and time outcomes together

segments.text: Okay, then what about the commute itself? You cannot skip getting home, so does commuting even have an opportunity cost?
Yes—both in route choice and in how you spend those minutes. A cheaper slower route trades extra minutes for lower fare.
And during the ride, scrolling social media versus listening to a study recap is another mini trade-off inside the same hour.
Fair point. Even when you cannot eliminate the constraint, seeing the implicit trade-off helps you spend scarce hours intentionally.
That is the core takeaway: every study, transit, and work choice carries an explicit price and an implicit next-best alternative.
